parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Define gravitational potential at a point.

markscheme_points.text: work (done in) moving mass from infinity (to the point)

hints: Hint 1: Think about what potential means in general - it is always energy shared out per kilogram, so focus on a tiny 1 kg test mass placed at the point.
Hint 2: Remember where we choose zero potential to be in gravity, and which journey the test mass must make to get to the point.
parts.proper_answer: The work done per unit mass in moving a mass from infinity to the point.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Potential means per kilogram**
Think of placing a 1 kg mass at that point in the field. Its gravitational potential energy divided by its mass is the potential. So you are really describing $\phi = E_p / m$, which is work done per unit mass.

Step 2: **Fix the starting point at infinity**
Gravity is always attractive, so work must be done by an external agent to bring a mass in from far away where the field is zero. By definition that start is at infinity. Putting both ideas together gives: work done per unit mass in moving a mass from infinity to the point.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.part_stem:
Mars is a planet that may be considered to be an isolated uniform sphere of radius $3.4 \times 10^{6}\text{ m}$.

A satellite of mass $122\text{ kg}$ is in orbit around Mars at a constant height of $1.7 \times 10^{6}\text{ m}$ above the surface of the planet.

The height of the orbit is increased to $6.8 \times 10^{6}\text{ m}$ above the surface. This increases the gravitational potential energy of the satellite by $5.1 \times 10^{8}\text{ J}$.
parts.text: Show that the mass of Mars is $6.4 \times 10^{23}\text{ kg}$.

markscheme_points.text: evidence of addition of $3.4 \times 10^{6}$ to $1.7 \times 10^{6}$ or $6.8 \times 10^{6}$

hints: Hint 1: The heights given are above the surface, but gravity acts from the centre of Mars - start by adding the planet radius to each height to get the two true orbital radii.
Hint 2: Recall how potential energy depends on $1/r$ for a point or spherical mass, so the increase is the difference between two $1/r$ terms multiplied by $GMm$.

Hint 3: Rearrange that energy difference to make $M$ the subject, then substitute $\Delta E_p = 5.1 \times 10^8 \text{ J}$, $m = 122 \text{ kg}$ and $G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \text{ SI}$ to check the value.
parts.proper_answer: $r_1 = 5.1 \times 10^6 \text{ m}$, $r_2 = 10.2 \times 10^6 \text{ m}$, $\Delta E_p = GMm(1/r_1 - 1/r_2) = 5.1 \times 10^8 \text{ J}$ giving $M = 6.4 \times 10^{23} \text{ kg}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Get radii from the centre**
A common slip is to use height alone. For a uniform sphere you must measure from the centre:
$$r_1 = 3.4 \times 10^6 + 1.7 \times 10^6 = 5.1 \times 10^6 \text{ m}$$
$$r_2 = 3.4 \times 10^6 + 6.8 \times 10^6 = 10.2 \times 10^6 \text{ m}$$

Step 2: **Write the change in potential energy**
Potential energy at radius $r$ is $E_p = -GMm/r$. Moving outward makes it less negative, so the increase is:
$$\Delta E_p = GMm\left(\frac{1}{r_1} - \frac{1}{r_2}\right)$$
Substitute the data:
$$5.1 \times 10^8 = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times M \times 122 \times \left[\frac{1}{5.1 \times 10^6} - \frac{1}{10.2 \times 10^6}\right]$$

Step 3: **Solve for M**
Evaluating the bracket gives $9.80 \times 10^{-8} \text{ m}^{-1}$. Hence:
$$M = \frac{5.1 \times 10^8}{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 122 \times 9.80 \times 10^{-8}} \approx 6.4 \times 10^{23} \text{ kg}$$
This confirms the stated value.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Calculate the gravitational potential $\phi$ at the surface of Mars. Give a unit with your answer.
hints: Hint 1: At the surface the distance to use is just the radius of Mars itself, not an orbital radius, and remember potential is negative because infinity is zero.
Hint 2: Check the form $\phi = -GM/r$ with your value of $M$ from (b)(i), and keep the unit as energy per kilogram.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Apply phi at the surface**
For a uniform sphere:
$$\phi = -\frac{GM}{r}$$
Here $r = R = 3.4 \times 10^6 \text{ m}$ and $M = 6.4 \times 10^{23} \text{ kg}$.

Step 2: **Calculate with correct sign and unit**
$$\phi = -\frac{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 6.4 \times 10^{23}}{3.4 \times 10^6}$$
$$\phi \approx -1.3 \times 10^7 \text{ J kg}^{-1}$$
The minus shows the field is attractive and zero is at infinity. The unit is joules per kilogram.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.part_stem: The satellite in (b) is moved to an orbit in which the satellite remains at the same point above the surface of Mars.
parts.text:
The orbit has a period of 25 hours.

State what can be deduced from this about the rotation of Mars on its axis.

markscheme_points.text: Mars takes (just under) 25 hours to rotate once on its axis

hints: Hint 1: If the satellite never moves relative to the ground below, what must be true about how fast the ground itself is turning underneath it?
parts.proper_answer: Mars rotates once on its axis in (just under) 25 hours.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link hovering to spin**
Staying over the same point means the satellite goes round at exactly the same rate as the planet turns below it. This is the Mars version of a geostationary orbit. So a 25 hour orbital period tells you the rotation period of Mars on its axis is also about 25 hours.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.text: State one other feature of this orbit.

markscheme_points.text: orbit is equatorial or orbit is in same direction as direction of rotation of Mars

hints: Hint 1: Picture the satellite trying to stay fixed over one spot - in which plane must it circle, and which way must it travel compared with the spin of Mars?
parts.proper_answer: The orbit is equatorial (and in the same direction as the rotation of Mars).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Conditions to stay fixed**
To remain over the same point, the satellite must circle above the equator, moving in the same direction as Mars rotates. Any tilted orbit or opposite motion would make it drift north-south or east-west across the sky.
